_readme: SEED facts gathered 2026-11-14 from web search results. Every fact is paraphrased and carries its source URL. verified_by_human is false for ALL of them: open each URL, confirm the numbers, then set it to true. Do not ship unverified facts. Replace weak/secondary sources with the primary page where noted.

facts.text_precise: On the ISS, astronauts' effective radiation dose builds up at roughly 0.2 to 0.5 millisieverts per day, about 40 to 90 millisieverts over a typical six-month mission.
facts.text_kids: Astronauts on the space station get a small dose of invisible space radiation every day. Over a six-month stay it adds up to a lot more than people get on Earth.
facts.source_name: NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS 20250006168, Simonsen et al., draft)
facts.note: Source is a draft PDF; confirm the final published numbers.

facts.text_precise: The U.S. DOE occupational limit for radiation workers is 50 millisieverts per year, and the general population receives about 3 millisieverts per year from natural background sources.
facts.text_kids: People on Earth get only a tiny amount of natural radiation each year. Astronauts get much more, so mission planners watch their dose carefully.

facts.text_precise: Neutron radiation makes up about 30% of the radiation astronauts receive on the ISS; early Radi-N2 results show about 150 microsieverts of neutron dose per day, with lower doses in the crew's sleeping quarters.
facts.text_kids: Some space radiation comes from tiny particles called neutrons. Where you sit or sleep inside the station changes how much you get.
facts.source_name: Canadian Space Agency, Radi-N2 experiment page
facts.note: Partner agency (listed in the challenge resources), not NASA. The comparison sentence about sleeping quarters was truncated in the search snippet: read the full page and word it exactly.

facts.text_precise: A lander on the far side of the Moon (Chang'E-4) measured an average daily radiation dose of about 1,369 microsieverts, roughly 2.6 times the ISS crew's daily dose.
facts.text_kids: On the Moon there is no air and no magnetic bubble to help, so the radiation dose per day is more than twice what astronauts get on the space station.
facts.source_name: Reported by Cosmos Magazine and WMUR about a Science Advances study (Chang'E-4 lander measurements)
facts.note: NOT NASA data and secondary reporting. Find the original Science Advances paper, replace source_url with it, and confirm the number.

facts.text_precise: In an OSDR-archived study, mice flown to the ISS lost significant muscle and bone mass during 33 days in microgravity; blocking myostatin/activin A signaling protected both muscle and bone.
facts.text_kids: When mice lived on the space station for a month, their muscles and bones got weaker. Scientists are testing ways to protect them, which could help astronauts too.
facts.source_name: NASA Open Science Data Repository dataset 10.26030/v2ak-0y21 (via data.gov catalog)
facts.note: Find the matching OSD study page on osdr.nasa.gov and use that URL if available.

facts.text_precise: In OSD-310 (STS-62, 14-day flight, ovariectomized rats), flown rats had 32% lower cancellous bone area in lumbar vertebrae than ground controls, with more bone resorption.
facts.text_kids: Even in a two-week space flight, rats lost some of the spongy bone in their spine compared with rats that stayed on Earth.
facts.source_name: NASA Open Science Data Repository, OSD-310
facts.note: Animal model with a specific condition (ovariectomized): do not present as a direct human result.

facts.text_precise: A study using OSDR data found spaceflight changes gene activity linked to inflammation and muscle wasting in mice and humans, similar to features seen in aging and frailty.
facts.text_kids: Living in space can make the body show some signs that look like getting older, such as weaker muscles. Scientists use this to plan how to keep astronauts healthy.
facts.source_name: NASA, Aging and Fragility Biomarkers are Altered by Spaceflight (part of the SOMA package in Nature)

gaps: No NASA source yet for shielding materials (e.g. hydrogen-rich materials, water). Search NASA pages; do not use opinion articles.
